findings.assertion: 1856 Ley Lerdo was a mechanism to assign corporate rental holdings to tenants by capitalizing annual rent at six percent; it explicitly included municipal and ecclesiastical corporations, not only church real estate.
geographies: Mexico City / legislation and property markets
findings.limitations: This is statutory text, not evidence that tenants actually acquired a specific Mexico City property; date variant June 23 in web header vs June 25 in decree catalogs.

findings.assertion: Article 8 of the 1856 Ley Lerdo exempted buildings immediately serving a corporation's purpose—including convents, schools, hospitals and markets—from the tenant-adjudication rule. Do not claim this statute by itself compelled wholesale demolition of convent buildings.
geographies: Mexico City / application of national law
findings.source_locator: Ley Lerdo transcription art.8, directly read.
findings.limitations: Subsequent separate decrees and the 1859 nationalization law changed legal status; no individual conveyance researched.

findings.assertion: A distinct presidential decree of 16 September 1856 ordered extension of Callejón de Dolores through the San Francisco convent toward San Juan de Letrán and suppression of the convent, following an alleged conspiracy. The conspiracy remains reported as real or supposed by the historian.
findings.source_locator: Monterrosa Prado, printed p.197 (PDF p.0) directly viewed; TRACE journal abstract; INAH monument catalog indexed history.
findings.limitations: Original decree and arrest reports not viewed; cannot assert conspiracy as proven; chronology of actual street works needs municipal files.

findings.assertion: The 12 July 1859 Juárez nationalization law made property administered by secular and regular clergy national property (article 1) and provided for separating government affairs from ecclesiastical affairs (article 3); it differed legally from the 1856 tenant-adjudication law.
geographies: Mexico City / national legislation amid civil war
findings.source_locator: 1859 transcribed decree arts 1-3; 1856 transcribed law arts 1-8.
findings.limitations: Both are later transcriptions; archival promulgation/implementation in Mexico City and legal disputes not independently examined.

findings.assertion: The 1859 decree ordered books, manuscripts, paintings, antiquities and other objects from suppressed religious communities to public museums, libraries and schools (art.12), while it initially permitted existing women's convents to continue (art.14); the latter makes immediate blanket closure of all nunneries in 1859 an error.
findings.period: Cultural property and gender in Reforma
geographies: Mexico City / religious collections and convents
findings.limitations: Specific inventory, transfers, resistance and later legal changes are not verified; law alone cannot establish actual destination for an artwork.

findings.assertion: The present 16 de Septiembre street crossing part of the former Convento Grande de San Francisco makes the loss of its original enclosure legible, but the 1856 decree and later road work must be distinguished; an on-site comparison requires a georeferenced pre-demolition plan.
findings.source_locator: Monterrosa Prado printed pp.197-198; INAH catalog indexed historical account.
findings.limitations: No certified 1856 property map, safe field route or exact corridor overlay; present street shape not independently surveyed.

findings.assertion: Monterrosa Prado reports that in 1861 Gante Street opened through the former San Francisco complex and chapels began to be demolished. A visitor can contrast Gante with the surviving religious buildings, but should not mistake modern lot boundaries for the 1861 deed lines.
geographies: Centro / Gante Street and San Francisco
findings.source_locator: Monterrosa Prado printed p.197; INAH indexed overview of block boundaries.
findings.limitations: Original 1861 municipal street-opening order, nine lot deeds and historic map not inspected; do not attribute every demolition to 1859 law alone.

findings.assertion: The entrance seen from Francisco I. Madero is described by the CDMX guide as the chapel of Balvanera entrance rather than the destroyed original central facade of the principal San Francisco church; the main facade was enclosed by later building on the Gante side.
findings.source_locator: CDMX official guide history (indexed); Monterrosa Prado printed pp.198-200; INAH indexed catalog.
findings.limitations: No field survey conducted and CDMX facade dating conflicts with some INAH guide details; do not claim full unchanged 18th-century facade.

findings.assertion: INAH's monument inventory distinguishes surviving components of the former San Francisco compound—church and Balvanera, a Methodist-used cloister and remains of the Calvario chapel—from lost chapels and sold parcels. A multi-stop field account needs separate current ownership and access checks.
geographies: Centro / Madero, Gante, Eje Central and 16 de Septiembre
findings.source_locator: INAH ficha 11735 index; official CDMX cultural guide.
findings.limitations: Survival status and accessible interiors not physically verified; no permit to enter private buildings; monument designation does not establish rights to images.

findings.assertion: Monterrosa Prado reports that later demolition revealed remnants attributed to the Chapel of Señor de Burgos, part of the main church facade and carved stone including a damaged Viacrucis relief; he compared these with Antonio García Cubas's historical plan. Reused older building fabric is physical evidence, not a complete reconstruction.
geographies: Centro / San Francisco formerly enclosed atrium
findings.source_locator: Monterrosa Prado printed pp.198-200, text directly inspected; page-image only first page 197 checked.
findings.limitations: Figure pages and physical finds not directly examined; source's excavation date lacks reliable independently confirmed journal year; do not say ruins are accessible today.

findings.assertion: Monterrosa Prado's comparison of an old stereoscopic photo with surviving entrances suggests the destroyed main church facade and an extant lateral portal had unusually similar designs; the article also reports destruction/reuse of facade sculptural elements. This remains an interpretation requiring photographs, dated surveys and later conservation records.
findings.source_locator: Monterrosa Prado printed pp.199-200; INAH monument catalog indexed note on rebuilt 1955 altarpiece.
findings.limitations: Original stereoscopic image not examined, source imagery rights unclear, existing facade modified; modern replica/retablo cannot be treated as original untouched fabric.
